inline_comments.comment: The two-line comment block here ('Only allow fallback to new Date() for timestamp formats (x, X)' / 'For all other formats, if dayjs strict parsing fails, throw an error') describes behavior that is **not implemented**. The `if (!isTimestampFormat(dateFormat))` branch immediately below it only emits an extra `log.debug` call — it does not throw, return early, or prevent the subsequent `const d = new Date(str)` from running for non-timestamp formats. Non-timestamp formats like `YYYY-MM-DD` still fall through to the `new Date()` fallback. The comment creates a false guarantee for future maintainers. Either implement the guard (e.g., `if (!isTimestampFormat(dateFormat)) { throw new Error('Invalid date:' + str); }`) or remove the misleading comment entirely.

`isTimestampFormat` is defined inside `getStartDate` and every call site passes the same outer-scope `dateFormat` variable. Since the function has no true closure dependency on `getStartDate`'s local state, it should be a module-level utility. This would also allow it to be reused by the renderer (e.g., in `makeGrid`) if needed, and would keep the function body of `getStartDate` focused on its single responsibility.

`MAX_TICK_COUNT = 10000` is introduced without any explanation for why 10,000 was chosen. Future maintainers or reviewers will have no way to evaluate whether the threshold is appropriate. Add a brief inline comment explaining the rationale, e.g.: `// Safety cap: rendering >10k axis labels causes measurable jank; D3 defaults are used instead.`

`getEstimatedTickCount` is declared as a nested function inside `draw`, but it has no closure dependencies on `draw`'s local variables — it operates entirely on its own parameters plus the module-level `dayjs` import. It should be extracted to module level, alongside the existing module-level `MAX_TICK_COUNT`. Module-level placement makes it independently testable (unit tests for the guard logic would be valuable), avoids re-creating the function object on every `draw` call, and makes it easier to reuse if a similar guard is ever needed in another code path.

The `interval ?? 'day'` fallback is misleading. The regex at line 654 only matches the exact set of valid unit strings (`millisecond|second|minute|hour|day|week|month`), so if `resultTickInterval` is non-null, `interval` is guaranteed to be one of those strings — never `null` or `undefined`. The `?? 'day'` is therefore dead code. More importantly, if an unrecognized unit were somehow passed (e.g., `'year'`), substituting `'day'` would compute a wildly incorrect estimate (365x too small for a `1year` interval), potentially allowing a genuinely excessive tick count through the guard. A safer fallback would be `return Infinity` for any unit not in the recognized set, or simply remove the nullish coalescing and rely on the upstream regex guarantee.

The entire block from line 659 to line 708 (bottom axis tick validation + switch) is duplicated nearly verbatim in the top axis block at lines 728–771. This is ~50 lines of near-identical logic, and this very PR already demonstrates the danger of the duplication: the two copies have diverged — the bottom axis logs a `warn` when the tick limit is exceeded, while the top axis silently skips (see the next comment). Extract a shared helper such as `applyTickInterval(axis, resultTickInterval, timeScale)` and call it for both axes.

When `estimatedTicks > MAX_TICK_COUNT`, the top axis block silently skips the custom tick interval with no user-visible or log-level feedback. The bottom axis block at line 676 correctly calls `log.warn(...)` explaining why the interval was dropped. Without a symmetric warning here, a developer or diagram author will see the bottom axis behave unexpectedly (using D3 defaults) while getting no indication in the console about why. The condition should be restructured to mirror the bottom axis: check `estimatedTicks > MAX_TICK_COUNT`, log the same warning, and fall through to the switch only in the `else` branch.

`expect(tasks[1].startTime.getFullYear()).toBe(202)` depends on `new Date('202-12-01')` parsing as year 202, which is V8/Node.js–specific behavior. ECMAScript specifies ISO 8601 date parsing, but `'202-12-01'` is not valid ISO 8601 (it has a 3-digit year). Non-conforming strings are implementation-defined. This assertion may pass in Node/Chrome but fail or return `NaN` in other environments (e.g., older Safari/WebKit or non-browser runtimes). Consider replacing the year assertion with a test that verifies the task _is_ parsed (i.e., `startTime` is a valid `Date` and is not `NaN`) rather than pinning the exact year value, which hardcodes fragile host-behavior assumptions.

general_comments.comment: The PR description states the root cause includes a 'Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) error.' A TDZ error requires accessing a `let` or `const` binding before its declaration within the same block scope. The original renderer code had `const every = resultTickInterval[1]` inside an `if` block — a straightforward const declaration with no TDZ risk. The description appears to misdiagnose the underlying bug. Accurately identifying the root cause matters: if the real cause was always and only 'the time domain can span billions of milliseconds when dates are invalid, producing an effectively unbounded tick generator,' the fix (capping estimated tick count) directly addresses that. But a misdiagnosis in the PR description can mislead future maintainers who search for this fix when debugging related issues.

The changes to `ganttDb.js` (`isTimestampFormat` helper, added comments) are cosmetic refactors that do not contribute to fixing the reported crash. The actual bug fix lives entirely in `ganttRenderer.js`. Bundling unrelated cosmetic changes with a crash fix makes the diff harder to review and understand, and risks introducing the misleading comment described in the inline comments above. Consider keeping non-functional refactors in a separate commit or PR.
